scope: employer of a worker; not stated; drilling incident with possible asbestos exposure, worker without a mask
rules: Where a worker may have been exposed to asbestos fibres in an incident, including working without proper respiratory protection, the exposure must be noted on their health record, or on their personal file if they have no health record.
An incident that releases asbestos fibres should itself be recorded.

scope: plumbing firm; not stated; removing old pipe lagging in an airing cupboard
rules: Removing or disturbing asbestos pipe lagging is licensable work that only a contractor holding an HSE licence may do.
Pipe lagging is a high-risk material because it releases fibres very easily, and wearing masks does not make the work non-licensed.

scope: not stated; not stated; drilling holes in a vinyl floor tile for a pipe
rules: Drilling a hole in an asbestos floor tile is lower-risk non-licensed work, so no licence is needed.
Maintenance work on vinyl or thermoplastic floor tiles is normally not notifiable, but workers still need non-licensed asbestos training and suitable controls.

scope: contractor; not stated; notifiable non-licensed asbestos work in tenants' flats
rules: For notifiable non-licensed asbestos work in domestic premises and on construction sites, the enforcing authority is HSE; local authorities enforce in premises such as shops, offices and hotels.

scope: contractor; not stated; removing textured coating strips in 30 flats on one estate over three months
rules: A programme of several notifiable non-licensed asbestos jobs in one local area, such as a housing estate, can be notified once for the whole programme instead of job by job.

scope: employer; not stated; workers doing notifiable non-licensed asbestos work
rules: For each worker doing notifiable non-licensed asbestos work, the employer must keep a health record (register) giving the type and duration of asbestos work, the estimated exposure and the dates of medical examinations.
The health record must be kept for 40 years.
The record can be as simple as noting the workers' names on the kept copy of the notification.

scope: employer; not stated; workers using disposable masks on asbestos jobs
rules: Tight-fitting respiratory facepieces, including disposable masks, must be face fit tested by a competent person when first selected, for the exact model and size the worker uses.
The fit test must be repeated when the mask model or size changes or the wearer's face changes significantly, such as weight change or dental work.
Wearers of tight-fitting masks must be clean-shaven where the mask seals.

scope: not stated; not stated; reoccupation of a tenanted flat after licensed asbestos removal
rules: After licensed asbestos work indoors, the area must pass a four-stage clearance (site completion check, detailed visual inspection inside the enclosure, air test, final check after the enclosure is removed) before a reoccupation certificate is issued; the air test is skipped for outdoor work.
The clearance must be carried out by an independent analyst accredited to ISO 17025.

scope: not stated (client or contractor); not stated; clearance after licensed asbestos removal
rules: Until 25 November 2027 the licensed removal contractor may appoint the accredited analyst for the clearance, although guidance strongly recommends the building client appoints the analyst.
From 25 November 2027 the employer responsible for the cleaning must not appoint the person who assesses the area for the reoccupation certificate.
From 25 November 2027 that assessor must be accredited to both ISO 17020 and ISO 17025.

scope: not stated; not stated; changes to the asbestos rules in 2026 and 2027
rules: The 2026 amendments to the asbestos rules mostly come into force on 25 November 2026, but the provisions starting then only update references to other laws.
The ban on the cleaning employer appointing the clearance assessor starts only on 25 November 2027, and the old rules apply until then.

scope: contractor; not stated; work inside housing association flats
rules: The duty to manage asbestos does not extend to the inside of private domestic flats.
Before work that may disturb asbestos, the employer must find out whether asbestos is present or presume that it is and act on that presumption.

scope: contractor; England (implied); kitchen refit in a home with no existing extractor
rules: When work is done in a kitchen, existing extract fans and cooker hoods venting outside should be kept or replaced.
If the kitchen had no ventilation system before, one need not be added, unless the work makes the home less compliant with the ventilation requirements than before.
Replacing an extractor fan or cooker hood on the existing cabling does not need to be notified to building control.

scope: contractor; England (implied); replacing all windows in an existing 1930s semi-detached house
rules: Replacement windows in an existing dwelling should achieve a U-value of 1.4 W/m2K or better, or a Window Energy Rating of Band B or better.
Replacement windows should be no worse in energy performance than the ones they replace.

scope: contractor; England (implied); single storey rear extension with large glazed doors and roof lanterns
rules: Under the simple elemental approach, the total area of windows, roof windows, rooflights and doors in an extension should not exceed 25% of the extension floor area plus the area of windows and doors lost or covered by the extension.

More glazing is allowed if the area-weighted U-value of the whole extension is shown to be no worse than a compliant extension of the same size, or a SAP calculation shows the home is no worse than with a notional extension.

scope: contractor; England (implied); kitchen extension over a public sewer
rules: Building over or within 3 m of a sewer shown on the sewer map needs a full plans application; a building notice cannot be used.
The sewerage undertaker that owns a public sewer must be consulted, and its permission is needed to build over or within 3 m of a sewer deeper than 3 m or larger than 225 mm diameter.

Unless the owner agrees, the length of sewer under the building should not exceed 6 m, and a manhole on a sewer serving more than one property should not be built over without other access being agreed.

scope: installer; England (implied); new gas boiler in a home kitchen
rules: When a new or replacement fixed gas appliance, other than one used only for cooking, is installed in a dwelling, a carbon monoxide alarm should be fitted in the same room.

The alarm should meet BS EN 50291-1 and be battery powered with a battery lasting the alarm's life and an end-of-life warning, or a hard-wired mains Type A alarm with a sensor failure warning, not a plug-in.
The alarm should be on the ceiling at least 300 mm from any wall, or high on a wall but not within 150 mm of the ceiling, and between 1 m and 3 m from the appliance.

scope: builder; England; 5 m single storey rear extension to a semi-detached house
rules: For a house that is not detached, a single storey rear extension is permitted development up to 3 m beyond the original rear wall and up to 4 m high.

Outside protected land and SSSIs it can extend up to 6 m only through the prior approval (neighbour consultation) process, and work cannot start until the council says approval is not needed, grants it, or 42 days pass without a decision.
Permitted development does not remove the need for building regulations approval.

scope: builder; England (implied); removing a chimney breast in a terraced house
rules: Removing a chimney breast affects the structure and may need building regulations approval.
Cutting away a chimney breast on a party wall needs a party structure notice served on the neighbour at least two months before the work starts, separately from building regulations.

scope: builder; England (implied); reusing reclaimed bricks in new extension walls
rules: Building work must use adequate and proper materials, which need not be new.
A material's fitness for purpose can be shown by past experience such as successful use in an existing building, or by tests, calculations or certification.

scope: contractor; England (implied); replacement windows in an existing old house
rules: The requirement for doors and windows to resist unauthorised access applies only to new dwellings, including those formed by a material change of use, not to replacement windows in an existing house.

scope: builder; England (implied); timber cladding on a two storey house extension
rules: The ban on combustible materials in external walls applies only to relevant buildings: those with a storey at least 18 m above ground level that contain dwellings, an institution or residential rooms.
An external wall outside the ban must still meet the general fire safety requirements for external walls.

scope: not stated; not stated; a staircase (type and building not stated)
rules: For a stair in a dwelling, each rise should be 150 to 220 mm and each going 220 to 300 mm, with a maximum pitch of 42 degrees.
Headroom over a dwelling stair should be at least 2 m, with a reduced headroom allowed for loft conversions.

scope: responsible person or landlord; England (implied); three-monthly fire door checks in a block of flats
rules: The three-monthly fire door checks are simple visual checks needing no tools, which caretakers, housing officers, managing agents or maintenance staff can do once shown how; no certified specialist is needed.
Repairs or replacements the checks identify must be carried out promptly by a competent contractor.
The routine checks do not replace periodic inspection of doors by fire specialists as part of the fire risk assessment.

scope: council landlord; England (implied); flat front doors in blocks of flats
rules: In a building with two or more sets of domestic premises, fire safety law covers the structure, the external walls, the common parts and all doors between the flats and the common parts.
The person responsible for the communal parts must carry out the fire door checks, and flat entrance doors count as common parts for this purpose.

scope: developer or contractor; England (implied); new block of flats about 13 m high
rules: Sprinklers are recommended in any block of flats with a top storey more than 11 m above ground.

Increasing the fire resistance of walls between flats beyond the recommended level is not an alternative to sprinklers, because it gives little benefit to occupants and none to those in the flat on fire.

scope: council or contractor; England; refurbishment of common parts in a council block (material alteration)
rules: The duty to hand over fire safety information on completion applies only to work that erects or extends a relevant building or forms part of a relevant change of use, not to a material alteration.
After the works, the responsible person must review the fire risk assessment.

scope: social landlord; England; significant hazard in a family's home not made safe in time
rules: If a significant hazard is not made safe within 5 working days (or an emergency hazard within 24 hours), the landlord must arrange suitable alternative accommodation at no cost to the household until the safety work is done, unless the tenant refuses it.
Whether the accommodation is suitable depends on the household's needs, such as number of bedrooms, distance to school and work, disability or medical needs, pets and the length of stay.

scope: social landlord; England; investigations of damp, mould and other hazards
rules: Hazard investigations under the social housing hazard rules do not require an HHSRS assessment, so the investigator needs no HHSRS qualification.

The investigator must be someone the landlord reasonably believes has the skills and experience to judge whether a significant or emergency hazard is present, with a suitably qualified person used where relevant, such as an electrician for an electrical hazard.

scope: landlord; England; re-letting an empty home with a three-year-old electrical report
rules: The electrical inspection before a new tenancy counts as done if an inspection was carried out in the previous 5 years and the report's next-due date has not yet passed.
The new tenant must be given a copy of the latest electrical inspection report before moving in.

scope: social landlord; England; flood from a tenant's own washing machine
rules: The landlord's repairing duty does not cover items the tenant is entitled to remove, such as their own washing machine, appliances that use the water or electricity supply, or repairs due to the tenant's duty to use the home in a tenant-like way.
The landlord's repairing duty still covers damage to the structure, and the hazard rules can apply if a building defect results in a significant or emergency hazard.

scope: landlord; England; tenant's claim that a flat is unfit for human habitation
rules: A landlord must keep the home fit for human habitation at the start of and throughout the tenancy, including common parts in which the landlord has an interest.

Fitness is judged on repair, stability, freedom from damp, internal layout, natural light, ventilation, water supply, drainage and toilets, facilities for preparing food and washing up, and any HHSRS hazard; no formal HHSRS assessment is required.
The duty does not cover problems caused by the tenant, damage by fire or flood, the tenant's own belongings, or work needing consent the landlord could not get despite reasonable efforts.

scope: social landlord; England (implied); tenant reports heating off
rules: Total loss of heating in cold weather where a vulnerable person lives is treated as an emergency hazard, to be made safe within 24 hours.
A home that cannot be kept warm enough can be a significant hazard, and the rules apply only where the heating system is the landlord's to repair.

scope: council landlord; England (implied); mould in a flat's bathroom
rules: An isolated patch of mould over a shower in a home with no vulnerable occupants is outside the hazard rules and is normal maintenance.
Widespread mould where occupants are vulnerable or have symptoms can be a significant or emergency hazard.

scope: contractor; UK; CIS monthly return and payment for the tax month ending 5 December
rules: The monthly CIS return must reach HMRC within 14 days of the end of the tax month, so by the 19th.

CIS deductions paid electronically must reach HMRC within 17 days of the end of the tax month (the 22nd, or the banking day before if that is not a working day), or within 14 days if paid by post or cheque.

scope: company with two directors; UK; applying for CIS gross payment status
rules: For gross payment status a company must show construction turnover, excluding VAT and materials, over the past 12 months of at least £30,000 per director or £100,000 for the company; a company controlled by five or fewer people needs £30,000 per person.
The applicant must also pass the business test (construction work in the UK, run through a bank account) and the compliance test (tax and National Insurance paid on time).

scope: contractor; UK; CIS changes from 6 April 2026
rules: From 6 April 2026 mainstream contractors must again file a nil monthly return for months with no subcontractor payments, unless they told HMRC in advance.
From 6 April 2026 payments to local authorities and listed public bodies are not contract payments, so they need no verification, deduction or reporting.

From 6 April 2026 anti-fraud rules make a business liable where it knew or should have known of deliberate non-compliance in the supply chain, with penalties up to 30%, immediate loss of gross payment status and a five-year wait before reapplying.

scope: contractor working for a property investment company; UK; refurbishment of let flats costing about £3.5m a year
rules: A business outside construction becomes a deemed contractor once its construction spending exceeds £3 million in a rolling 12-month period.
The exemption for work on a business's own premises does not cover property held for letting or as an investment.

scope: builder; UK; building a granny annexe that cannot be sold separately from the main house
rules: An annexe that cannot be lived in or disposed of separately from the main house does not meet the 'designed as a dwelling' conditions, so its construction is not zero-rated and is standard-rated at 20%.

scope: contractor working for a developer; UK; converting an office block into four flats
rules: Converting non-residential premises such as offices into dwellings, or changing the number of dwellings, is a qualifying conversion charged at the reduced 5% rate.
Such a conversion is zero-rated only when done for a relevant housing association.

scope: contractor or subcontractor; England and Wales (implied); sub-contract with no payment terms
rules: Where a construction contract of 45 days or more has no payment terms, interim payments fall due on the later of 7 days after the end of each period (28 days if no period is set) and the payee's claim.
The final date for payment is 17 days after the due date.
The final payment falls due 30 days after completion or the payee's claim, whichever is later.

scope: contractor; UK (implied); four-week construction contract with a subcontractor
rules: A party to any construction contract, however short, has the right to refer a dispute to adjudication.
The 45-day duration only decides whether a party is entitled to stage payments; contracts with a residential occupier are excluded from the statutory rights.

scope: contractor; England; district council works contract worth about £180,000
rules: For a regulated contract below the threshold, an authority inviting tenders must not use a separate suitability assessment stage, such as financial or technical pre-qualification, to filter bidders.
That ban does not apply to works contracts at or above £207,720 for local authorities (£135,018 for central government), and the authority may still consider suitability when assessing tenders.

scope: contractor; UK; bidding for central government contracts over £5 million a year
rules: Bidders for central government contracts worth more than £5 million a year must show effective supply chain payment systems, meeting a standard of 95% of invoices paid within 60 days.

scope: contractor; UK; paying a new subcontractor under CIS
rules: A contractor must verify a subcontractor with HMRC before paying them for the first time, using their UTR, NI number or company details and registered name.
The deduction is 20% for a registered subcontractor, 30% if unregistered or not matched, and nothing if they have gross payment status.
The deduction applies only to the labour part of the payment, after excluding the subcontractor's materials, hired plant and VAT.

scope: builder; UK; a house job (type of work not stated)
rules: Building work on existing buildings is normally standard-rated at 20%.

Building a new dwelling can be zero-rated; converting non-residential premises into homes or changing the number of dwellings is usually 5%, and renovating a home empty for at least 2 years can be 5%.

scope: builder as the only contractor; Great Britain (implied); kitchen extension for a homeowner
rules: A homeowner having work done on their own home, not in connection with a business, is a domestic client.
On a domestic project with only one contractor, the client duties pass to that contractor in addition to its own contractor duties.

scope: principal contractor; Great Britain (implied); homeowner project with an architect
rules: A domestic client may agree in writing for the principal designer to carry out the client duties.
Without that written agreement, the client duties pass to the principal contractor, even if the designer coordinates the project.

scope: contractor; Great Britain (implied); refurbishing housing association flats
rules: Housing associations, councils, landlords and other businesses that own homes are not domestic clients; they are commercial clients and carry the client duties in full.
Only a person having work done on their own or a family member's home, not in connection with a business, is a domestic client.

scope: builder; not stated; small domestic building site
rules: A site must have readily accessible toilets that are clean, lit and ventilated.
Washing facilities with running hot and cold or warm water, soap and towels must be provided next to the toilets.
Drinking water, changing and drying facilities where special work clothing is worn, and rest facilities with tables, chairs with backs and the means to boil water and prepare food must be provided.

scope: decorator or builder; not stated; two days painting soffits and fascias on a two storey semi-detached house
rules: A ladder may be used for work at height only where a risk assessment shows more suitable equipment is not justified because the risk is low and the use is short, or because of site features that cannot be changed.
Short duration means roughly 15 to 30 minutes in one position for light work.
Collective protection such as a tower or scaffold must be chosen in preference to personal protection.

scope: not stated; not stated; use of ladders on building sites
rules: Ladders are not banned; a ladder may be used where a risk assessment shows the risk is low and the use is short or site features cannot be changed.
A ladder in use must be secured against slipping.

scope: roofer or builder; not stated; replacing a few slipped tiles on a pitched roof
rules: For short-duration work on a pitched roof, decided by a risk assessment, the minimum is safe access to roof level plus a purpose-made, supported roof ladder.
The roof ladder should span at least three rafters and be secured over the ridge by a proper anchorage, not by bearing on the ridge tiles.

scope: employer; not stated; workers using breakers for hours
rules: For hand-arm vibration the daily exposure action value is 2.5 m/s² A(8) and the exposure limit value, which must not be exceeded, is 5 m/s² A(8).
In the points system, 100 points a day equals the action value and 400 points the limit value.
Workers exposed at or above the action value, or otherwise at risk, must be under health surveillance.

scope: employer; not stated; choosing ear defenders
rules: Hearing protection must be chosen to bring exposure below the exposure limit values.
Hearing protection should aim for 70 to 80 dB(A) at the ear and avoid bringing levels below 70 dB(A), because over-protection stops people hearing warnings and each other.

scope: builder; not stated; digging footings near buried cables and gas pipes
rules: Work that could strike buried services must not start until suitable precautions are taken, such as getting service plans, locating services with a cable avoidance tool and marking the route.
Mechanical excavators and power tools should not be used within 0.5 m of the suspected line of a buried service.

scope: builder; not stated; chasing a wall near a circuit said to be switched off
rules: Precautions such as locking off must be taken to stop isolated electrical equipment being made live again during the work.
A verbal assurance is not enough: the isolated circuit must be proved dead by a competent person with a suitable test instrument, such as a two-pole voltage detector checked before and after use.

scope: not stated; not stated; work on live electrical equipment
rules: Work on or near live conductors is allowed only when all three conditions are met: it is unreasonable for the equipment to be dead, it is reasonable for the person to work on it live, and suitable precautions, including protective equipment where needed, are taken.
A person may do such work only if they have the technical knowledge or experience, or the supervision, needed to prevent danger.

scope: contractor; not stated; workers paid as self-employed under CIS
rules: A worker treated as self-employed for tax can still count as an employee for health and safety law.
A contractor must plan, manage, monitor and supervise work done by workers under its control, and an employer must ensure people not in its employment are not put at risk.

scope: contractor; not stated; 1.5 m trench supported with trench boxes
rules: A competent person must inspect a supported excavation at the start of each shift, after any event likely to affect its strength or stability, and after any accidental fall of material, and be satisfied it is safe before work continues.
If the inspector is not satisfied, they must tell the person in control before the end of the shift and give a written report within 24 hours, which must be kept on site and then for 3 months.

scope: not stated; not stated; a construction job (size not stated)
rules: A construction project must be notified if it is planned to last more than 30 working days with more than 20 workers at the same time, or to exceed 500 person days.
Every day on which work is done counts towards the working days, including weekends.

scope: contractor; not stated; kitchen refits in 20 council flats in a block
rules: A management survey is not enough before refurbishment where it was not intrusive in the areas to be disturbed; a refurbishment survey is then required.
A refurbishment survey is fully intrusive in the areas where work will take place.
Where only certain rooms such as kitchens are being upgraded, the refurbishment survey can be limited to those rooms.

scope: contractor; not stated; bathroom work in a tenant's flat with no asbestos survey or register
rules: Before work that could disturb asbestos, the employer must find out whether asbestos is present, its type, the material and its condition, or else presume it is present and is not white asbestos (chrysotile) alone.

Where asbestos is presumed, the material is treated as blue or brown asbestos and the full rules apply, including a licensed contractor where the work requires one; work should not start without a suitable survey or register.

scope: contractor; not stated; work in a home where the survey marked the loft hatch area and the void behind the bath as no access
rules: Areas a surveyor could not access must be presumed to contain asbestos unless there is strong evidence otherwise, and no work that could disturb them should be done there until they have been checked.
A refurbishment survey must gain access to any areas marked as no access in an earlier survey.

scope: not stated; not stated; unsampled painted AIB ceiling tile with a few scratches in a hallway
rules: In the material assessment, asbestos insulating board scores 2 as a product type, a few scratches or minor damage scores 1 as low damage, and painted or sealed AIB scores 1 for surface treatment.
A material that has not been sampled and analysed is scored as crocidolite, which scores 3 for asbestos type.
A total material assessment score of 7 to 9 means a medium potential to release fibres if disturbed.

scope: contractor; not stated; drilling in flats built in 2003
rules: Construction after 1999, when nearly all asbestos products had been banned, can be used as evidence that a material is unlikely to contain asbestos; the risk is higher in buildings built or refurbished before 2000.
The duty to assess whether asbestos is present before work that could disturb it still applies, so the build date must be reliable and no older materials reused.

scope: contractor's worker; not stated; suspect grey board found above a ceiling in a riser
rules: When suspect asbestos material is found unexpectedly, work must stop at once, the area be kept clear of people, and the person in charge be told.
The material must then be sampled and analysed, or presumed to be the most hazardous type of asbestos and the matching controls used, including a licensed contractor if the work requires one.

scope: contractor; not stated; accidental drilling of a suspect panel in an occupied flat, dust released, tenant nearby
rules: After an uncontrolled release of asbestos, the employer must at once take steps to reduce its effects and restore control, warn anyone who may be affected, and keep out everyone not needed to deal with it.

A worker lightly contaminated should stay put, damp-wipe and remove outer clothing, which with used rags is disposed of as asbestos waste; dust must not be swept but cleaned by a suitable method, and the event recorded.

scope: contractor; not stated; clearing up a few chunks of AIB knocked off a cupboard panel
rules: Clearing up a small release of AIB in fairly intact, separate pieces will probably not need a licensed contractor, and the same applies to firmly bound materials such as asbestos cement.
Clearing up releases of lagging, loose fill, sprayed coatings, a large release of AIB, or anything where exposure could exceed the control limit needs a licensed contractor.

scope: contractor; not stated; removing and refitting a screwed AIB bath panel to replace pipes
rules: Removing and refitting a loosely fixed, for example screwed, AIB panel to get access for other maintenance such as pipework under a bath is non-licensed work that is not normally notifiable.
Non-licensed asbestos work still needs trained workers, a risk assessment, a plan of work and suitable controls.

scope: contractor; not stated; removal of a small AIB partition in a flat during refurbishment, about 1.5 hours with two workers
rules: Work is short duration only if no one worker does more than one hour and all workers together do no more than two hours in any seven days.
Short duration removal of AIB during a refurbishment is normally notifiable non-licensed work, needing notification, marking out of the area, medicals and health records.
AIB work that is not short duration needs a licensed contractor.

scope: electrician; not stated; drilling an Artex ceiling to fit a light
rules: Drilling textured decorative coatings to fit fixtures is non-licensed work that is not normally notifiable.
Workers doing non-licensed asbestos work must have task-specific non-licensed training and use a suitable work method.

scope: contractor; not stated; stripping a whole Artex lounge ceiling with steamers
rules: Removing textured coating with steam or gel over a large area, beyond small areas for fitting smoke alarms or lights, is normally notifiable non-licensed work because the method breaks the material down.
Notifiable non-licensed work must be notified before it starts, the work area marked out, and workers given medicals and have health records kept.

scope: contractor; not stated; after a non-licensed Artex strip inside an enclosure
rules: For non-licensed asbestos work there is no requirement for a clearance air test or an independent certificate of reoccupation.

After significant non-licensed jobs such as stripping textured coating, the area must be thoroughly cleaned and visually checked, and the contractor gives the occupier a written statement that it is clean and fit to reoccupy.

scope: contractor; not stated; removing asbestos cement sheet roofs from a row of estate garages
rules: Removing asbestos cement sheets carefully without breaking them, even if weathered, is non-licensed work that is not normally notifiable.
Where the sheets are badly damaged by fire or flood, or the method will break them up, such as dropping the roof, the work becomes notifiable non-licensed work.
Asbestos cement roofs are fragile, so nobody should walk directly on them and a safe system of work over them is needed.

scope: contractor; not stated; lifting probable asbestos vinyl floor tiles by hand under kitchen lino
rules: Removing asbestos floor tiles and their adhesive by hand is non-licensed work for trained workers.
If the tiles are backed with asbestos paper or the work will substantially break them up, it becomes notifiable non-licensed work.
Removing asbestos flooring by grinding needs a licensed contractor.

scope: contractor; not stated; removing Artex from a ceiling where the boards underneath are AIB
rules: Removing coatings that cover AIB is licensable work for a licensed contractor.
The non-licensed treatment of textured coatings covers only the coating, not the board under it, which may itself be AIB.

scope: contractor; not stated; notifying notifiable non-licensed asbestos work
rules: Notifiable non-licensed work must be notified to HSE using its online form, not by phone or letter, before the work begins.
There is no minimum notice period and no need to wait for a reply or approval before starting.

scope: employer; not stated; workers starting notifiable non-licensed asbestos work for the first time
rules: Workers doing notifiable non-licensed work must have a medical before they start and then at least every three years while they continue that work.
The medical can be done by any registered doctor such as a GP and must include a chest examination and a lung function test.
The medical is in work time at the employer's cost, and the doctor's certificate must be kept for four years.

scope: employer; not stated; medicals for notifiable non-licensed asbestos work
rules: An HSE-appointed doctor is required only for licensed work; the medical for notifiable non-licensed work can be done by any registered medical practitioner, such as a GP.

scope: employer; not stated; plasterers and electricians not intending to work on asbestos
rules: Anyone whose work could disturb the fabric of a building, such as plasterers, electricians, plumbers, joiners and decorators, and those who supervise them, must have asbestos awareness training.
The only exception is where the employer can show the workers only ever work in buildings free of asbestos.

scope: employer; not stated; workers with awareness training removing asbestos floor tiles
rules: Asbestos awareness training only helps workers avoid disturbing asbestos and does not prepare them to work on it.

Workers who will knowingly disturb asbestos in non-licensed work, notifiable or not, need additional task-specific training covering risk assessment, controls, RPE, waste, emergencies and which work must be notified.

scope: employer; not stated; asbestos awareness training refreshers
rules: There is no legal requirement to repeat a full formal awareness course every 12 months, and a certificate expiry date does not in itself mean full retraining is needed.
Refresher awareness training is still needed when appropriate and can be less formal, such as e-learning or an in-house talk by a competent manager or supervisor.

scope: employer; not stated; workers doing non-licensed asbestos work
rules: Refresher training for non-licensed asbestos work is needed every year, or sooner if methods or control equipment change, the work changes significantly, or gaps in competence appear.
Refresher training should be based on a training needs analysis and can be a toolbox talk or online module, with practical parts such as RPE use and decontamination where needed.

scope: contractor's workers; not stated; clearing up asbestos debris after drilling
rules: Asbestos dust and debris must never be swept; it must be cleaned with a Class H vacuum cleaner or damp rags.
Asbestos waste must be double bagged in suitable asbestos waste bags, kept separate from general waste, and disposed of at a licensed site.

scope: contractor; not stated; bagging and storing waste from a non-licensed asbestos job
rules: Asbestos waste must be sealed in suitable labelled bags or wrapping as it is produced; two plastic sacks are suitable for most waste, with stronger packaging for sharp pieces.
Labels on asbestos waste must follow the carriage of dangerous goods rules or the prescribed asbestos label.
Sealed waste not removed straight away must be kept in a secure, clearly marked store such as a lockable skip.

scope: contractor; not stated; full strip-out of a block of flats with joinery and asbestos removal at the same time
rules: Before demolition or major refurbishment, the written plan of work must say that asbestos is removed before other major works begin, so far as reasonably practicable, unless removal would create a greater risk than leaving it.
Removing asbestos first also makes sense in smaller refurbishments that change the structure or layout.

scope: client or main contractor; not stated; licensed removal of pipe lagging in a plant room
rules: Licensable asbestos work must be notified in writing to the enforcing authority at least 14 days before it starts, unless the authority agrees to a shorter period.
Any material change to notified licensable work must be notified in writing without delay.

scope: scaffolding contractor; not stated; erecting scaffold for licensed removal of AIB soffits
rules: Work with asbestos includes ancillary work, such as erecting and striking scaffolding for access, where it could foreseeably disturb or damage the asbestos.
Ancillary work needs a licence whenever the main asbestos work is licensable.

scope: contractor asking about the dutyholder; not stated; stairwells and roof space of a council block of flats
rules: The duty to manage asbestos applies to the common parts of multi-occupancy domestic premises, such as stairs, lifts, plant rooms and roof spaces, but not to the inside of individual flats.
The dutyholder is whoever has the obligation to maintain or repair the premises under a lease, tenancy or contract, usually the council or housing association.

scope: not stated; not stated; asbestos exposure limits
rules: The asbestos control limit is 0.1 fibres per cm3 averaged over 4 hours.
Exposure is not sporadic and low intensity if it exceeds 0.6 fibres per cm3 measured over 10 minutes.
Work where exposure is liable to exceed the control limit or is not sporadic and low intensity is licensable.

scope: contractor; not stated; several small AIB removals during one refurbishment
rules: Where several asbestos activities form part of a larger job such as a refurbishment, they must be considered together, not one by one, when deciding whether the work is notifiable non-licensed work.
Short duration work counts the time of all workers together over any seven days.

scope: contractor; not stated; non-licensed asbestos job in an occupied flat with another firm's electrician present
rules: An employer's asbestos duties extend, so far as reasonably practicable, to other people affected by the work, such as other contractors, residents and visitors, and the risk assessment and plan must allow for them.
People on the premises must be told what they need to stay safe, and employers sharing a workplace must co-operate.

scope: self-employed plasterer; not stated; not stated
rules: A self-employed person has the duties of both an employer and an employee under the asbestos regulations, including being properly trained.

scope: contractor; not stated; removing an old fire door containing AIB from a flat
rules: Removing a door with AIB fireproofing is non-licensed work for trained workers.
Asbestos waste, including such a door, must be sealed or wrapped and labelled as asbestos waste, not put in an ordinary skip.

scope: builder with a Gas Safe registered engineer; not stated; replacing a combi boiler in a home
rules: Installing a gas appliance or heating system by a Gas Safe registered installer is self-certification work, so no building notice or full plans application is needed.
The installer must, within 30 days of completion, give the occupier a compliance certificate and give the building control authority notice or the certificate.

scope: builder; not stated; like-for-like bathroom suite replacement in a home
rules: Replacing a toilet (with one using no more water), basin, fixed bath or shower needs no building notice or full plans, provided there is no work to underground drainage and nothing done to the water supply or above-ground drainage that could affect health or safety.

scope: builder and plumber; not stated; new shower room with new plumbing in an upstairs bedroom of a house
rules: A plumber registered with a competent person scheme can self-certify a new toilet, basin, shower or bathroom in a dwelling only if the work does not involve shared or underground drainage; otherwise a building notice or full plans is needed.
A new bathroom needs extract ventilation of 15 litres per second if intermittent.

scope: builder; not stated; adding an en-suite to an existing home
rules: When a wet room is added to an existing dwelling, provide either an intermittent extract fan of 15 l/s with a background ventilator of at least 5000 mm2, or continuous mechanical extract, or a single-room heat recovery unit.
Internal doors should allow air to pass, equal to a 10 mm undercut on a standard 760 mm door: 10 mm above the floor finish, or 20 mm above the bare floor if the finish is not yet fitted.

scope: window installer; not stated; replacing windows without trickle vents in a house
rules: When windows without background ventilators are replaced, ventilation must be no worse than before, for example background ventilators of at least 8000 mm2 in habitable rooms and kitchens and 4000 mm2 in bathrooms, or 4000 mm2 per habitable room and none in wet rooms if there is continuous mechanical extract.
Where the old windows had background ventilators, the new ones must be no smaller and must be controllable.

scope: builder with an unregistered window fitter; not stated; replacing all windows in an existing house
rules: Replacing windows in an existing dwelling is building work that can be self-certified only by an installer registered for it with an authorised competent person scheme.
If the installer is not registered, a building notice or full plans application must be given to the building control body before work starts.

scope: builder; not stated; new house extension
rules: New thermal elements in an extension to an existing dwelling should meet limiting U-values of 0.15 W/m2K for roofs, 0.18 for walls and 0.18 for floors.

A lesser wall standard may be accepted where meeting it would reduce a room's floor area by more than 5%, and the floor U-value may be calculated using the perimeter and area of the whole enlarged dwelling.

scope: builder; not stated; loft conversion of a house with retained roof slopes and gable walls
rules: Retained elements in a loft conversion should be upgraded where worse than the threshold: a roof worse than 0.35 W/m2K improved to 0.16, and a wall worse than 0.70 improved to 0.30.

Where that is not technically or functionally feasible or would not pay back within 15 years, the element should be upgraded as far as feasible within a 15-year payback, generally to no worse than 0.7.

scope: builder; not stated; stripping and re-plastering the back wall of a solid brick terraced house
rules: Stripping a wall back to the bricks and re-plastering or dry-lining it counts as renovating a thermal element, which is notifiable work.

If more than 50% of the element's surface is renovated, the whole element should be upgraded, to 0.30 W/m2K for a wall with internal insulation, as far as technically, functionally and economically feasible.
A lesser standard may be acceptable where insulation would reduce the room's floor area by more than 5% or would not pay back within 15 years.

scope: roofer or builder; not stated; replacing the membrane on a flat roof garage extension
rules: Replacing the waterproof membrane of a flat roof counts as renovating a thermal element, and if more than 50% of the roof is renovated the whole roof should be upgraded to 0.16 W/m2K where feasible.
Replacing a roof covering is notifiable, but a roofer registered with a competent person scheme can self-certify it instead of a building notice being given.

scope: builder; not stated; stair for a loft conversion in a house
rules: For a private stair, each rise should be 150 to 220 mm and each going 220 to 300 mm, with a maximum pitch of 42 degrees.
Twice the rise plus the going should be between 550 and 700 mm, and all steps in a flight should have the same rise and going.

scope: builder; not stated; loft conversion stair with limited headroom under the roof slope
rules: The normal clear headroom over a stair is 2 m, but in a loft conversion without space for that, 1.9 m at the centre line falling to 1.8 m at the side of the stair is acceptable.

scope: builder; not stated; new spindles and handrail on a stair in a family house
rules: Handrail tops should be 900 to 1000 mm above the pitch line or floor, with handrails on both sides of stairs 1000 mm or wider.
Guarding on a stair or landing in a dwelling should be at least 900 mm high.
Where children under five may use the building, guarding should not let a 100 mm sphere pass through any opening and should be hard to climb.

scope: builder; not stated; glazed back door with side panels and a low window
rules: Critical locations are glazing in doors and side panels near doors between floor level and 1500 mm, and glazing in windows and walls between floor level and 800 mm.
Glazing in critical locations must break safely (for example Class 3 to BS EN 12600 or Class C to BS 6206), be robust, be in small panes or be permanently protected.
Door and side panel panes wider than 900 mm in critical locations need the higher Class 2 or Class B safe breakage standard.

scope: builder; not stated; strip footings for an extension on clay near large trees
rules: Strip foundations not on rock should be at least 0.45 m deep to avoid frost damage.
On shrinkable clay the minimum depth is 0.75 m for low, 0.9 m for medium and 1.0 m for high shrinkage clay, and footings may need to go deeper near trees or to reach good ground.

scope: builder; not stated; new extension external wall
rules: A damp-proof course in an external wall should be at least 150 mm above the adjoining ground, unless the wall is protected by another part of the building, and continuous with the floor damp-proof membrane.
In a cavity wall the cavity should extend at least 225 mm below the lowest damp-proof course, or a damp-proof tray be used.

scope: builder; not stated; fitting a wood burner into an existing fireplace in a lounge
rules: Installing a solid fuel appliance can be self-certified by an installer registered with a competent person scheme; otherwise building control must be notified.
A carbon monoxide alarm should be fitted in the room where a solid fuel appliance is installed.
Where a hearth, fireplace or flue is provided or extended, a permanent notice plate giving the key hearth and flue details should be fixed.

scope: heating installer; not stated; boiler-only replacement in an existing home keeping radiators and pipes
rules: Designing a wet heating system for a maximum 55 C flow temperature applies when the system is newly installed or fully replaced (boiler, emitters and pipework), not to a boiler-only swap.
A gas boiler for wet central heating in an existing dwelling should have an ErP seasonal efficiency of at least 92%.
The heating system should be sized from a heat loss calculation and not oversized.

scope: electrician; not stated; kitchen refit with sockets added to an existing ring and a new oven radial in a home
rules: In a dwelling, only three kinds of electrical work are notifiable: installing a new circuit, replacing a consumer unit, and adding to or altering a circuit in a special location such as a room with a bath or shower.
All electrical work in a dwelling, notifiable or not, must still meet the electrical safety requirement, for example by following BS 7671.

scope: electrician not registered with a competent person scheme; not stated; replacing a consumer unit in a home
rules: Replacing a consumer unit is notifiable electrical work.

A non-registered installer can appoint a registered third-party certifier before starting, notify them within 5 days of completion so they inspect and test, with the certificate sent to the occupier and building control within 30 days.
Alternatively the installer notifies building control before work begins, and building control decides what inspection and testing it needs.

scope: builder; not stated; single storey extension
rules: With full plans, the building control body must decide within 5 weeks, or 2 months if agreed, giving formal approval before building.
With a building notice, work can start 2 days after giving it, there is no formal approval, and the authority can ask for plans later.
Full plans must be used where the building is covered by the Fire Safety Order, fronts a private street, or the work is over or near a mapped sewer.

scope: builder; not stated; starting an extension after full plans approval
rules: Work must not start until the building control authority has been told of the intention to start and at least two days have passed after the day the notice was given.
A commencement notice must be given within five days after the work is treated as commenced, and the authority can reject it within four weeks if it disagrees.
Work on a horizontal extension is treated as commenced once the foundations and the ground floor structure are complete.

scope: property owner; not stated; loft conversion done earlier without approval
rules: Unauthorised work done on or after 11 November 1985 can be regularised by applying to the local authority, not a private approver, for a regularisation certificate.
The local authority may require work to be opened up or tested and further work done, and has no duty to issue the certificate.
The regularisation charge must be paid with the application or the application is not valid.

scope: main builder; not stated; large domestic loft conversion with several contractors and no written duty-holder appointments
rules: If a domestic client does not appoint them, the designer in control of the design phase is the principal designer and the contractor in control of the construction phase is the principal contractor.
Where a domestic client has more than one contractor, the client's duties pass to the principal contractor, or to the principal designer if they agree that in writing with the client.

scope: building firm doing extensions, windows and boilers; not stated; Future Homes Standard changes
rules: The amended Part L and Part F rules apply from 24 March 2027, or 24 September 2027 for higher-risk buildings.
For work on existing homes the limiting U-values stay the same, for example windows 1.4 W/m2K, walls 0.18 and roofs 0.15 for new elements.
Work notified before 24 March 2027 stays under the old rules only if it starts before 24 March 2028.

scope: builder; not stated; extension with a building notice given in February 2027 and a start in spring 2028
rules: The old rules continue only where the building notice, initial notice or full plans was given before 24 March 2027 and the work starts before 24 March 2028; otherwise the amended rules apply.
Work on an extension counts as started only when the foundations and the ground floor structure are complete.

scope: not stated; England; bathroom extract fan
rules: A bathroom needs a minimum intermittent extract rate of 15 l/s, unchanged between the 2021 and 2026 ventilation guidance.
The 2026 ventilation guidance takes effect on 24 March 2027 for work that is not higher-risk building work.

scope: builder; England; new downstairs toilet next to a kitchen in a house
rules: A room containing a toilet must be separated from a kitchen or food preparation area.
In a dwelling, a toilet room that also has a hand basin needs only a door between it and the kitchen, not a separate lobby.
If the toilet room has no basin, the hand washing space must be entered before the food area and be separated from it by a door.

scope: builder; England; loft conversion with new bedroom and shower room in a house
rules: New internal floors, and internal walls between a bedroom or a room containing a WC and other rooms, should achieve at least 40 dB Rw airborne sound insulation (laboratory value).
The internal sound insulation requirement does not apply to internal walls containing a door, or to a wall between an en-suite toilet and its own bedroom.

scope: builder or building owner; England and Wales; loft conversion in a terraced house, cutting into the party wall for a beam
rules: Cutting into a party wall, for example to bear a beam, is work for which a party structure notice must be served on the adjoining owner at least two months before the start date.
If the adjoining owner does not consent in writing within 14 days of the notice, a dispute is deemed to have arisen and is settled by surveyors.
A party structure notice lapses if the work does not start within 12 months of its service.

scope: builder or building owner; England and Wales; rear extension foundations near a neighbour's building
rules: Excavating within 3 m of a neighbour's building to a depth below the bottom of its foundations needs a notice served at least one month before starting, stating whether the owner proposes to underpin or protect the neighbour's foundations.
Within 6 m of a neighbour's building, a notice is needed where the excavation would cut a line drawn downwards at 45 degrees from the bottom of the neighbour's foundations.
If the neighbour does not consent within 14 days of the notice, a dispute is deemed to have arisen.

scope: builder or building owner; England and Wales; party wall or excavation work after notice served
rules: If the adjoining owner does not consent in writing within 14 days of a party wall or excavation notice, a dispute is deemed to have arisen and must be settled by surveyors through an award.
If the adjoining owner fails to appoint a surveyor when asked, the building owner may appoint one on their behalf.
Notified work may not start before the notice period (one month or two months) ends unless the adjoining owner agrees in writing.

scope: builder or householder; England; rear dormer loft conversion on a mid-terrace house
rules: Under permitted development, a roof enlargement on a terraced house must not add more than 40 cubic metres to the original roof space (50 cubic metres for other houses), including earlier roof extensions.
A dormer is not permitted development on a roof slope forming the principal elevation that fronts a highway, or on article 2(3) land.

Permitted development roof extensions must use similar-looking materials, be set back about 0.2 m from the eaves where practicable, have no balcony, and have side-facing windows obscure glazed and non-opening below 1.7 m above floor level.

scope: builder or householder; England; ground-level conservatory of about 12 m2 at the back of a house
rules: A ground-level conservatory or porch with a floor area of no more than 30 m2 is exempt from building regulations, provided its glazing meets the safety glazing requirements.

An exempt conservatory must keep thermal separation from the house; if that separation is removed or the heating system is extended into it, it is treated as an extension and the energy requirements apply.
Electrical work in an exempt conservatory is still subject to the electrical safety requirement.

scope: builder or householder; England; detached timber garden building of about 20 m2, 0.5 m from the boundary, with power from the house
rules: A detached single-storey building of up to 15 m2 floor area with no sleeping accommodation is exempt from building regulations.
A detached building between 15 m2 and 30 m2 with no sleeping accommodation is exempt only if it is at least 1 m from the boundary or built substantially of non-combustible material.
Electrical work in an exempt detached building is still subject to the electrical safety requirement.

scope: customer and boiler installer; England; boiler installation under self-certification
rules: A self-certifying installer must give the occupier a copy of the compliance certificate, and give the building control authority notice or the certificate, within 30 days of completing the work.

scope: builder or owner; England; building work on a building that is not higher-risk, already started without notice
rules: For work that is not on a higher-risk building, the person may use either the local authority or a registered building control approver, and an approver gives the local authority an initial notice.

Work that has already started or finished without notification cannot be taken on by a private approver; only the local authority can deal with it, through regularisation, and it is not obliged to approve it.

scope: builder; England; bathroom refit with new bath in an existing house
rules: The 48 C limit on hot water delivered to a fixed bath applies only where a dwelling is newly built or formed by a material change of use, not to a refit of an existing dwelling.
Where the 48 C limit applies, it is usually met by an in-line blending valve or similar device with a maximum temperature stop.

scope: builder; England; rear extension to a house
rules: The basic accessibility requirement for dwellings and its guidance apply to new dwellings and to dwellings undergoing material alteration, not to extensions of a dwelling.
Where a material alteration is made to a dwelling, it should be no less compliant with the basic accessibility requirement than before the work.

scope: builder; England; new downstairs toilet in a house
rules: The toilet accommodation requirement for universal toilets applies to buildings other than dwellings, not to toilets in houses.
In a dwelling, toilets are covered by the sanitation requirement: at least one WC and hand basin, separated from the kitchen.

scope: builder or owner; England and Wales; loft conversion with party wall work and planning and building regulations approval
rules: The party wall regime is separate from planning permission and building regulations, so those approvals do not remove the duty to serve party wall notices for covered work.
The local council has no duty to tell a building owner about the party wall regime.
If notifiable party wall work starts without notice, the adjoining owner can seek a court injunction.

scope: builder; England; house extension with a driveway
rules: Electric vehicle charge point requirements apply only to new residential buildings, buildings undergoing a material change of use into dwellings, and major renovations where the building will have more than 10 associated parking spaces; a house extension is not covered.

scope: builder; England; loft conversion with large rooflights in an existing house
rules: The overheating requirement applies only to new residential buildings, not to a loft conversion in an existing house.
Additional glazing in work on an existing dwelling is still limited by the energy efficiency requirements.

scope: builder; England (assumed); not stated
rules: Building regulations apply to building work: new buildings, extensions, material alterations, provision or extension of controlled services or fittings, material changes of use, cavity wall insulation and underpinning.
Some small works are exempt or do not need notice, and work by a person registered with a competent person scheme needs no building control application.

scope: builder; England (assumed); not stated
rules: Limiting U-values depend on the element and the type of work: for example 0.18 W/m2K for new walls in an extension to a dwelling.
A renovated existing wall with internal insulation should reach 0.30 W/m2K, and replacement windows in an existing dwelling 1.4 W/m2K.

scope: builder or building owner; England and Wales; not stated
rules: Building a new wall on the boundary line needs a notice at least one month before starting.
Work to an existing party wall, such as cutting into it or raising it, needs a party structure notice at least two months before starting.
Excavating within 3 m, or within 6 m where a 45 degree line is cut, of a neighbour's building to below its foundation level needs a notice at least one month before starting.

scope: contractor; England; replacing flat front doors in a council block of flats
rules: A flat entrance door between a flat and a common corridor or lobby should be a 30-minute fire doorset with smoke control (E 30 Sa, or FD 30S under the BS 476-22 test).
Every fire doorset, including flat entrance doors, should be fitted with a self-closing device.
From 2 September 2029 the BS 476 test route is removed and only the European classification is listed.

scope: council as landlord; England; existing 14-storey council block of flats
rules: In a building with two or more flats whose top storey is above 11 m, the responsible person must use best endeavours to check flat entrance doors at least once every 12 months and must check fire doors in the communal areas at least once every 3 months.
The fire door checks must include checking that self-closing devices work.
The responsible person must keep a record of the checks, including the steps taken where access to a flat was not obtained.

scope: council as responsible person; England; existing block of flats with top storey above 11 m, resident refusing access
rules: The annual flat entrance door check is a best-endeavours duty, so failing to gain access is not automatically a breach.
The responsible person must record the steps taken to try to gain access in each 12-month period.

scope: contractor or inspector; England; checking self-closers on fire doors in a block of flats
rules: A self-closer works if the door, released from fully open and again from about 15 degrees open, closes fully into its frame each time, overcoming the latch and any floor resistance.
Routine fire door checks must include checking that self-closing devices work.

scope: contractor or responsible person; England; corridor fire doors held open on alarm-linked magnets in a block of flats
rules: When checking a held-open fire door, release it with the test button where provided rather than pulling it off the hold-open device.
A self-closing fire door may be held open only by an automatic release device triggered by the building's fire detection and alarm system, so smoke detection must be present.
The weekly fire alarm test should also check that alarm-linked door releases let the doors close.

scope: contractor advising a council; England; existing 1970s flat entrance doors in a council block
rules: An existing flat entrance door that fits its frame well and met the fire door standard of its day may be kept; upgrading with intumescent strips, smoke seals and a fire-protected letterbox suits only a solid door of adequate thickness (around 44 mm); otherwise it can be replaced with a certified FD30S door.
Flat entrance doors and doors protecting corridors and stairs need a positive-action self-closing device; rising butt hinges are not adequate.

scope: contractor quoting to a council; England; existing flat entrance doors in a block of flats
rules: The fire door check regulations do not require existing doors to be brought up to the standard for new buildings; a door that met the standard of its day is usually adequate if undamaged and with acceptable gaps, and missing strips, seals or certificates alone do not make it inadequate.
Whether an existing fire door is adequate is a matter for the fire risk assessment, and nothing requires replacement just because a door falls short of current building regulations.

scope: responsible person; England; existing 4-storey block of flats with top floor about 9 m
rules: The annual flat entrance door checks and 3-monthly communal fire door checks apply only where the top storey is above 11 m.
The duty to give residents fire door information applies to every building with two or more flats and common parts used for escape, whatever its height.
Below 11 m the responsible person must still keep fire doors adequate under the general fire safety duties.

scope: not stated; England; internal doors off the hallway inside a flat
rules: Doors forming part of a protected hallway or landing within a flat should give 20 minutes' fire resistance.
Self-closing devices are not needed on fire doors within flats, even where those doors give lobby protection to a common stair.

scope: council as responsible person; England; block with two or more flats
rules: In a building with two or more flats and common parts used for escape, residents must be told to keep fire doors shut when not in use, not to tamper with self-closers, and to report any fault or damage to fire doors to the responsible person straight away.
This fire door information must be given to new residents as soon as reasonably practicable after they move in and to all residents at least once every 12 months.

scope: contractor; England; pipes through a compartment wall between a flat and the corridor
rules: A pipe passing through a fire-separating element (outside a protected shaft) should use one of three methods: a proprietary tested sealing system; fire-stopping around the pipe with the opening as small as possible and the pipe within the maximum diameters for the situation; or, for lead, aluminium, fibre-cement or uPVC pipes up to 160 mm, a sleeve of non-combustible material that will not melt in a fire.
Openings for services should be few, as small as practicable, and fire-stopped in a way that allows thermal movement of the pipe.

scope: contractor; England; 110 mm uPVC soil stack through a compartment floor between flats
rules: A uPVC stack through a compartment floor between flats can be up to 160 mm diameter with simple fire-stopping only if it is enclosed in a drainage enclosure with a casing of at least E 30 that is not sheet metal.
Where the pipe is not so enclosed, the 40 mm limit for any other situation applies, so a larger pipe needs a proprietary tested seal or the sleeving method.

scope: contractor; England; cables through a riser wall opening
rules: Openings for cables should be as few and as small as practicable and must be fire-stopped.

Fire-stopping spanning more than 100 mm unsupported, or using non-rigid materials without suitable fire test evidence, should be reinforced or supported by class A2-s3, d2 or better material so it cannot be dislodged.

scope: not stated; England; gas riser in the stairwell of a block of flats
rules: Gas pipes and meters should not be placed in a protected stairway unless installed in accordance with the 1996 pipelines safety regulations and the 1998 gas safety (installation and use) regulations.

In a protected shaft, natural gas or LPG pipes should be screwed or all-welded steel installed to those regulations, and a shaft carrying piped gas must be ventilated to open air at both top and bottom.

scope: contractor; England; retrofitting fire stopping on plastic waste pipes in an occupied existing block of flats
rules: In existing blocks, pipes below about 40 mm are not normally a concern, but larger, especially combustible, pipes passing through compartment walls or floors should be protected with proprietary seals or collars or fire-resisting boxing, which may only be practicable over time as flats become empty.
Checking fire stopping within flats usually needs opening up, which is done only in destructive (Type 2 or Type 4) fire risk assessments.

scope: contractor; England; kitchen and bathroom programme in occupied council flats
rules: Landlords should include fire precautions in building contracts, check method statements and inspect while work is in progress, including small jobs.
Hot work should be controlled by a permit-to-work system, with checks of the area before and after and fire extinguishers to hand.

Contractors must not leave holes through compartment walls or floors, remove or prop open stair doors, block fire main inlets, leave gas cylinders inside overnight or store combustible materials in common parts.

scope: repairs contractor to a council; England; council housing premises
rules: The fire safety duties of the responsible person also apply to any other person who has any control over the premises, to the extent of the matters within their control.
A person with a contractual obligation to maintain or repair the premises, or for their safety, is treated as having control to the extent of that obligation.

scope: council as landlord; England; council tenant's flat
rules: Since 1 October 2022 social landlords as well as private landlords are covered by the smoke and carbon monoxide alarm duties.

The landlord must ensure a smoke alarm is fitted on each storey with a room used as living accommodation, check the alarms work on the day a new tenancy starts, and repair or replace an alarm once told it is faulty.

scope: landlord; England; rented home with a gas hob in the kitchen
rules: The carbon monoxide alarm duty does not apply to gas cookers; an alarm is needed in a room used as living accommodation only if it contains another fixed combustion appliance, such as a gas boiler or a wood burner.

scope: council as landlord; England; tenant reporting a faulty smoke alarm
rules: Once a tenant reports a smoke alarm as faulty, the landlord must check it and repair or replace it if it is not working, as soon as reasonably practicable.
This repair duty applies to reports made from 1 October 2022.

scope: council as social landlord; England; council flats
rules: Since 1 October 2022 any immediate landlord of a covered tenancy, including a social landlord, is a relevant landlord bound by the smoke and carbon monoxide alarm duties.
A local authority cannot enforce the alarm rules against itself, but it is still bound by them.

scope: council; England; leaseholder's flat in a council block
rules: Long leases and tenancies granting occupation for 7 years or more are excluded tenancies, so the smoke and carbon monoxide alarm duties do not apply to them.
The alarm duties do not cover owner-occupied or shared-ownership homes; they apply only to covered rented tenancies.

scope: responsible person; England; communal fire alarm in a block of flats
rules: A communal fire alarm system should be tested weekly by operating a call point, including any linked actions such as door hold-open releases.
The fire alarm system should be serviced by a competent person at least twice a year, following BS 5839-1.

scope: responsible person; England; existing 20-storey residential block of flats
rules: In a residential building at least 18 m high or with at least 7 storeys, the responsible person must check monthly that firefighting lifts, evacuation lifts and essential firefighting equipment are working.

If a fault in a lift or key firefighting equipment is not fixed within 24 hours, the local fire and rescue service must be told electronically as soon as reasonably practicable, and told again once it is fixed.

scope: responsible person; England; residential block of flats
rules: In a residential building at least 18 m high or with at least 7 storeys, the responsible person must install and maintain a secure information box holding their name, UK address and phone number, details of others with access, and paper copies of floor and building plans, and inspect the box at least once a year.
For new building work, a secure information box is recommended in any block of flats with a top storey more than 11 m above ground.

scope: not stated; England; new block of flats
rules: Sprinklers should be provided throughout any block of flats with a top storey more than 11 m above ground, designed to BS 9251 for residential buildings.
Sprinklers are needed within the flats, but not in common stairs, corridors or landings that are kept fire sterile.

scope: designer or contractor; England; new blocks of flats with a storey at 18 m or more
rules: From 30 September 2026, a block of flats with a storey 18 m or more above ground should have at least two common stairs.

The previous guidance continues to apply where a building notice, initial notice or full plans were deposited before 30 September 2026 and the work was sufficiently progressed before that date or within 18 months after it.
For work to an existing building, the work is sufficiently progressed once it has started.

scope: not stated; England; fire safety guidance for building work
rules: From 2 March 2025 the fire safety guidance updated handover information under regulation 38, removed old BS 476 reaction-to-fire and roof classifications and required sprinklers in all new care homes, with a 6-month transitional period.
From 30 September 2026 the guidance requires at least two common stairs in blocks of flats with a storey at 18 m or more and covers evacuation lifts, with an 18-month transitional period.
From 2 September 2029 BS 476 fire resistance classifications are removed, leaving only European classifications, with a 6-month transitional period.

scope: contractor; England; overcladding an existing 12 m council block of flats
rules: In a residential building with a storey 11 m or more above ground, insulation and filler materials in external walls should be class A2-s1, d0 or better, except in masonry cavity walls built to the specified detail.
In a relevant building with a storey 18 m or more above ground, all materials in the external wall must be class A2-s1, d0 or A1, apart from the listed exemptions.

scope: not stated; England; existing 8-storey block of flats about 17 m to the top floor
rules: A building is a higher-risk building if it is at least 18 m high or has at least 7 storeys and contains at least two residential units.
Height is measured from ground level to the top of the floor surface of the top storey, and storeys below ground and roof-top plant storeys are ignored when counting storeys.

scope: not stated; England; block with a basement car park, 6 floors of flats and a roof garden
rules: When counting storeys for higher-risk status, storeys below ground are ignored, and a storey is below ground if any part of its ceiling is below the adjacent ground.
An open roof garden is not treated as a storey and is not used for measuring height.

scope: not stated; England; two 8-storey council towers joined by a shared underground car park
rules: Attached structures count as one building unless they contain independent sections; a section is independent if it has an entrance and exit reachable from anywhere in it and either no access to other sections or access only to sections with no residential units.
Doors used only in an emergency or for maintenance do not count as access between sections.

scope: contractor; England; fire stopping and communal door upgrades in an existing registered higher-risk building
rules: Building work to an existing higher-risk building needs building control approval from the Building Safety Regulator before it starts, unless it is exempt work, competent person scheme work or emergency repairs.

Work affecting passive fire protection or common parts is category A work, so the application must include extra documents such as a competence declaration, construction and change control plans, a mandatory occurrence reporting plan, a compliance statement and fire and emergency file.
The regulator should decide the application within 8 weeks unless a longer period is agreed in writing.

scope: contractor and client; England; urgent fire stopping repair in a riser of a higher-risk building
rules: Emergency repairs needed because of a risk to people's health, safety or welfare may start without prior approval from the Building Safety Regulator where getting approval first is not practicable.
For emergency repairs the client must notify the regulator of the work and why it was urgent, send a copy to the fire safety responsible person, and afterwards apply for regularisation.

scope: contractor; England; work to meet a fire service enforcement notice on a higher-risk building
rules: Work needed to comply with a fire service enforcement notice will rarely count as an emergency repair, because it does not need to start straight away, so prior approval from the Building Safety Regulator is usually needed.

scope: landlord or accountable person; England; occupied higher-risk residential tower
rules: In an occupied higher-risk building, residents aged 16 or over and owners must not act in a way that creates a significant building safety risk and must not interfere with relevant safety items in the common parts without reasonable excuse.
The accountable person can serve a contravention notice on a resident who breaches these duties and may require payment of the reasonable cost of repair or replacement.
Residents must be told regularly not to tamper with fire door self-closers.

scope: council as responsible person; England; block of flats after refurbishment of the common parts
rules: The fire risk assessment must be reviewed when there has been a significant change in the matters to which it relates, such as alterations, or when there is reason to suspect it is no longer valid.
Since October 2023 the whole fire risk assessment must be recorded, including the name of anyone who helped carry it out.

scope: council as responsible person; England; block with two or more flats
rules: In a building with two or more domestic premises, residents must be given comprehensible information on the risks identified by the fire risk assessment, the fire safety measures, the responsible person's name and UK address, who assisted with the assessment, any nominated competent persons, and risks notified by other responsible persons.

Fire safety instructions, including the evacuation strategy and how to report a fire, must be displayed in a conspicuous place and given to new residents and to all residents at least every 12 months.

scope: contractor and residents; England; fire safety remediation of an occupied residential block
rules: Most residents can stay at home during remediation, and the building owner, agent or landlord must tell residents whether it is safe to stay, using temporary measures such as alarms, extra fire wardens or a changed evacuation strategy where needed.
Residents may need to leave temporarily if the fire risk is serious, if urgent work cannot be done safely while occupied, or if the fire service or council judges the building unsafe.

scope: builder; England; extension to a block of flats
rules: The person carrying out the work must give fire safety information to the responsible person no later than completion, or first occupation if earlier where the extension was unoccupied during the work.
The responsible person must confirm receipt, and the person carrying out the work must then notify the building control body within 5 days (30 days under a competent person scheme).

The fire safety information should include as-built plans showing escape routes, fire-resisting construction, fire doors and self-closers, detection and alarm equipment, sprinklers and smoke control, with equipment specifications and maintenance schedules.

scope: designer; England; new block with evacuation lifts
rules: An evacuation lift should be in an evacuation shaft that also contains a protected stair and an evacuation lift lobby, with the lobby serving as a refuge and opening directly onto the protected stair.
The evacuation lift lobby must not open directly from flats, storage rooms or electrical rooms.
Where the protected stair has smoke control, the evacuation lift and its lobby should be given the same smoke control protection.

scope: not stated; not stated; fire doors in a building, type and height not stated
rules: In a block of flats with a top storey above 11m, the responsible person must use best endeavours to check flat entrance fire doors at least once a year.
In a block of flats with a top storey above 11m, communal fire doors must be checked at least every 3 months.
Below 11m no check interval is set, but the responsible person must still keep fire doors maintained in efficient working order and good repair.
