scope: contractor or social landlord; England; Awaab's Law hazard in a social rented home
rules: For an emergency hazard the landlord must investigate and complete any make-safe work within 24 hours of becoming aware; otherwise the investigation must be finished within 10 working days, counting from the day after awareness.
The tenant must get a written summary within 3 working days after the investigation ends, unless all required work is already finished.

For a significant hazard, make-safe work must be done within 5 working days of the investigation; preventative work must start or steps be taken within 5 working days, actually start within 12 weeks and finish in a reasonable period; if the home cannot be made safe in time, suitable alternative accommodation must be offered at the landlord's cost.

scope: contractor or social landlord; England; emergency hazard (water through ceiling) in a social rented home
rules: For an emergency hazard the landlord must investigate and complete any make-safe work within 24 hours.
The 24-hour period starts as soon as the landlord has reasonable grounds to believe an emergency hazard exists, not the day after.
Where another law sets a shorter timeframe for the same repair, the shorter one applies.

scope: contractor or social landlord; England; damp and mould in a social rented home
rules: A significant hazard is one that a reasonable landlord with knowledge of the household's health and circumstances would act on within 15 working days, but not within 24 hours.

Damp and mould is significant where the occupiers are likely to suffer serious health effects, including worsening of existing conditions, if it is not dealt with in time; small isolated patches with no likely serious harm are normally out of scope.
There are no fixed thresholds; extent, location, duration, ventilation and insulation and the household's vulnerability are weighed.

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; damp report under Awaab's Law
rules: Only working days count, excluding weekends, Christmas Day, Good Friday and bank holidays in England and Wales.
Day 1 of the 10 working day investigation period is the day after the landlord became aware, so a Friday report has day 1 on the next working day (normally Monday).

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; written summary after an Awaab investigation
rules: The written summary must be given within 3 working days, with day 1 the day after the investigation ends.

It must state whether a significant or emergency hazard was found and what it is, any further action required with target start and finish dates, or if none is needed that fact and the reasons, and how the tenant can contact the landlord.

scope: contractor; England; burst waste pipe repaired same day in a social rented home
rules: No written summary is required if all the work the investigation identified, both make-safe and preventative, is completed within the 3 working day period.
The tenant must still be told that the work has been completed.

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; mould report assessed from photos
rules: Where the investigation had no physical inspection and no preventative work has started, a tenant's request triggers a renewed investigation that must include an in-person inspection and be completed within 10 working days, counted from the day after the request.
A renewed investigation is not needed if preventative work has already started or emergency safety work or a further investigation applies.

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; damp from a damaged roof needing scaffold
rules: The home must be made safe within 5 working days after the investigation and kept safe afterwards.

Supplementary preventative work must start within 5 working days or, if not reasonably practicable, steps to start it must be taken in that time, with the work starting as soon as reasonably possible and within 12 weeks at most, and finished within a reasonable period.

scope: social landlord; England; tenant refuses temporary accommodation during dangerous ceiling repair
rules: Once the household refuses an offer of suitable alternative accommodation, the landlord need not keep offering it unless circumstances change materially.

Where occupiers stay in the home, the landlord must give written safety advice by the make-safe deadline or as soon as reasonably practicable after: what occupiers can do to reduce the risk, or that nothing they do will reduce it to a tolerable level, plus any steps that still help.

scope: social landlord; England; rehousing a household under Awaab's Law
rules: The household is the tenant and family members who normally live in the home in line with the tenancy.
A child under 18 counts if a household member has caring responsibilities for them and the child usually stays overnight at least once a week and would have done so during the rehousing period.

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; tenant blocking access for a damp survey
rules: The tenant must allow the landlord or its authorised contractor access for Awaab work at reasonable times on at least 24 hours' written notice.
The landlord has a defence if it shows it took all reasonable endeavours to meet the requirements.

scope: repair contractor for a housing association; England; mould spotted during a tap repair
rules: If the contractor is in law the landlord's agent, the landlord may be treated as aware when the contractor learns of the hazard; otherwise awareness starts when the contractor reports it to the landlord.
If the operative is the landlord's own employee, the landlord is aware when the employee is told of the hazard.

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; mould where tenant blocked bathroom extractor
rules: A hazard wholly or mainly caused by the tenant's breach of the tenancy, such as blocking ventilation fans, is outside Awaab's Law.
If the real cause is a building deficiency such as missing ventilation or poor insulation, it is in scope and the landlord must address it.

scope: housing association; England; district heating failure maintained by the freeholder
rules: A hazard is in scope only if it arises from a defect in something the landlord is responsible for repairing or maintaining; a district heating system the landlord has no duty to maintain is out of scope.
The landlord should still take reasonable steps to get the problem fixed, such as raising it with the freeholder.

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; boiler failure in January for an 80-year-old tenant
rules: A boiler failure in cold winter weather affecting an elderly tenant is an emergency hazard, which must be investigated and made safe within 24 hours.
People over 65 are at higher risk from cold, and weather and whether any room can be heated must be considered.

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; loose patio slab, tenant in her thirties
rules: A loose patio slab is out of Awaab scope where the fall risk is low because the area can be avoided and the household has no vulnerabilities, so it is a normal repair.
The assessment changes where the household includes people at higher fall risk, such as young children, older people or people with mobility problems.

scope: gas engineer or council landlord; England; no working smoke alarm in a council flat with young children
rules: No working smoke alarm inside the home is an emergency hazard requiring action within 24 hours, likely whatever the household.
Awaab's Law covers fire hazards inside individual homes but not fire risks in common parts covered by the Fire Safety Order.

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; damaged communal fire door in a tower block
rules: Fire hazards from defects in the parts of a multi-occupied building covered by the Fire Safety Order, including common parts and doors between flats and common parts, are excluded from Awaab's Law.
Such defects must be reported to the building's Responsible Person (or acted on if the landlord is the Responsible Person).

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; EICR with only C3 codes and old consumer unit
rules: A C3 code means improvement is recommended but the installation is satisfactory, and the landlord is not required to act on it.
An undamaged consumer unit with only a C3 is out of Awaab scope, but the household's circumstances can make it significant (for example a pregnant tenant with a young child and several C3s).

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; damaged socket with exposed live parts, toddler in home
rules: A damaged socket with accessible live parts and a young child in the home is an emergency hazard that must be investigated and made safe within 24 hours.
The investigation must be carried out by a person with the right competence, normally a qualified electrician for an electrical hazard.

scope: contractor; England; timing of remaining HHSRS hazards under Awaab's Law
rules: The remaining HHSRS hazards will be added in a later phase for which no fixed date has been set.
Emergency hazards of any HHSRS type except crowding are already covered, but non-emergency hazards of the remaining types are not yet.

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; unsafe cladding on a block
rules: Neither make-safe work nor preventative work under Awaab's Law includes cladding work.
The landlord must still meet the other Awaab duties, such as investigating, doing other non-cladding safety work and keeping the tenant informed.

scope: repairs contractor for a housing association; England; general needs, shared ownership and supported housing
rules: Awaab's Law applies to social housing let on a tenancy by a registered provider, including supported or temporary housing held on a tenancy.
It does not apply to homes occupied under a licence, shared ownership or other low-cost home ownership, or long leases.

scope: contractor; England; record keeping on Awaab jobs
rules: The landlord has a defence if it can show it took all reasonable endeavours, which it proves through records.
Clear records should be kept of all contact, investigations, access attempts, tenant vulnerabilities, photos of the hazard before work and safety advice given.

scope: not stated; England; HHSRS hazard categories
rules: A hazard score of 1,000 or more falls in the High band and is a category 1 hazard; scores in the Medium and Low bands are category 2.
The score is based on the likelihood of harm needing medical attention in the next year to the most vulnerable age group and the spread of possible harm across classes.
Councils must take action on category 1 hazards and have a power to act on category 2.

scope: surveyors; England; HHSRS assessments
rules: The amended HHSRS reduces the hazards from 29 to 21 by merging several, and replaces letter bands with High, Medium and Low bands.
The changes came into force on 23 June 2026 and apply to council inspections begun on or after 22 June 2026, in England only.

scope: repairs contractor for a council; England; council-owned housing
rules: A council has no power to take HHSRS enforcement action against itself as landlord of its own homes.
This does not protect homes managed by an ALMO, a tenant management organisation or another social landlord.

scope: contractor; England; social housing to the current Decent Homes Standard
rules: A decent home must meet four criteria: no category 1 HHSRS hazards, reasonable repair, reasonably modern facilities and reasonable thermal comfort.
A home fails the modern facilities test only when three or more of the listed items are missing (such as a kitchen 20 years old or less, a bathroom 30 years old or less).
A home fails the repair test if a key component, or two other components, are past their lifetime and in poor enough condition to need major work.

scope: contractor; England; 25-year-old kitchen in good condition in a social rented flat
rules: A kitchen over 20 years old is only one missing item, and a home fails the modern facilities test only when three or more items are missing.
A component fails the repair test only if it is both past its standard lifetime (30 years for a kitchen) and in poor condition; age alone does not fail a home.

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; electrical testing in social housing
rules: The fixed electrical installation must be inspected and tested by a qualified person before each tenancy and then at intervals of no more than 5 years, or sooner if the report says so.
For social tenancies that began before 1 December 2025, the first inspection and test was due by 1 November 2026.
The tenant must get a copy of the report within 28 days, and the council within 7 days of asking.

scope: not stated; England; landlord's repairing duty for a rented home
rules: The landlord must keep the structure and exterior in repair, including drains, gutters and external pipes.
The landlord must keep in repair and working order the installations for water, gas, electricity, sanitation, space heating and water heating, but not appliances using those supplies.

For a flat the duty extends to parts of the building and installations the landlord has an interest in where disrepair affects the tenant, and the standard depends on age, character, prospective life and locality.

scope: surveying contractor; England; stock condition surveys for a housing association
rules: A registered provider must hold a current, accurate condition record for every individual home based on a physical assessment of each one.
No fixed survey frequency is set; it depends on factors such as age, construction, archetype and complaints and repairs data.

scope: repairs contractor to a registered provider; England; Competence and Conduct Standard
rules: The standard is placed on registered providers, who must take appropriate steps to ensure people working for their service providers, including contractors, are competent and behave appropriately, and set out how in a written policy.
Qualification requirements reach a service provider's managers only where it delivers a full housing management service for the landlord.

scope: repair operatives; England; mould removal in homes
rules: Surface mould should be removed with a mould and mildew product rather than bleach, using goggles, gloves and a mask, with larger areas done by qualified professionals.
Removing surface mould is not a substitute for fixing the underlying cause.

scope: contractor; England; diagnosing damp before quoting
rules: Damp can be condensation, penetrating, rising or traumatic, and there may be more than one cause.

Diagnosis should rest on an in-person inspection by qualified people with external and internal checks; rising damp should be confirmed by testing such as chemical analysis because it is often misdiagnosed.

scope: contractor; England; damp report under Awaab's Law
rules: A standard investigation must be completed within 10 working days, with day 1 the day after the landlord becomes aware; the 14 calendar day figure is not the final rule.
Emergency hazards have a separate 24-hour deadline.

scope: surveyor or social landlord; England; damp scored category 2 under HHSRS
rules: A hazard does not need to be HHSRS category 1 for Awaab's Law to apply.
The Awaab test looks at the actual household: a hazard is significant if a reasonable landlord knowing the household would act within 15 working days, and emergency if within 24 hours.

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; mould affecting a baby's breathing
rules: Tenants do not have to provide medical evidence, and action must not be delayed waiting for it; reported vulnerability should generally be taken at face value.
Damp and mould affecting a young child who already has symptoms points to an emergency hazard.

scope: social landlord or contractor; England; serious mould in an overcrowded flat
rules: Overcrowding itself is outside Awaab's Law, but other hazards made worse by overcrowding are not.
Mould that is a significant or emergency hazard must still be made safe and prevented within the Awaab deadlines.

scope: not stated; England; flat assessed against Decent Homes
rules: Under the current standard a decent home must meet all four criteria: no category 1 HHSRS hazards, reasonable repair, reasonably modern facilities and reasonable thermal comfort.
The new Decent Homes Standard applies from 2035.

scope: contractor; UK; paying a subcontractor registered for net payment under CIS
rules: A registered subcontractor who is verified has deductions made at the standard rate of 20%.
The deduction applies only to the labour part: VAT, materials, consumables, hired plant and non-travel fuel come off first.

scope: contractor; UK; unmatched CIS verification of a plasterer
rules: If HMRC cannot match the subcontractor, the contractor must deduct at the higher rate of 30%.
The deduction statement for a higher-rate deduction must show the verification reference HMRC gave.

scope: contractor; UK; re-engaging a bricklayer last paid in March 2024
rules: A subcontractor need not be verified only if he was included on the contractor's CIS return in the current tax year or the two previous tax years; otherwise he must be verified before payment.

scope: contractor; UK; re-engaging a groundworker paid gross in July 2025
rules: No verification is needed if the subcontractor was on a CIS return in the current or two previous tax years.
The contractor pays on the same basis as last time and may assume the status is unchanged unless HMRC says otherwise.

scope: contractor company in a group; UK; paying an electrician used by a sister company
rules: Verification is not needed if another company in the same group verified the subcontractor or included him on a return in the current or two previous tax years.
Companies are in a group for this purpose if one owns at least 75% of the other or a third company owns at least 75% of both.

scope: contractor; UK; pricing a job with a subcontractor
rules: A contractor may verify a subcontractor only once there is a contract with him or his tender has been formally accepted.

scope: contractor; UK; invoice from a non-VAT-registered tiler with materials
rules: For a subcontractor who is not VAT registered, VAT he paid on materials counts as part of the materials cost.
The CIS deduction is 20% of the payment after the materials cost is taken off.

scope: contractor; UK; groundworker using his own mini digger
rules: Plant hire can be taken off before the CIS deduction only where the subcontractor actually hired the plant from a third party; there is no notional hire charge for plant he owns.
Fuel used by the plant in the work can still be treated as materials.

scope: contractor; UK; subcontractor invoice with travel fuel and accommodation
rules: Travel costs, including fuel for travel, and subsistence such as accommodation are part of the gross payment and subject to the CIS deduction.
Only materials, consumables, hired plant, fuel used in the work (not for travel) and prefabrication are deducted before the 20% is applied.

scope: contractor; UK; amount withheld from a subcontractor for poor work
rules: Money withheld because the contractor believes the subcontractor breached the contract is a set-off that reduces the payment, so the CIS deduction is worked on the reduced amount.
A contra charge for goods or services supplied to the subcontractor does not reduce the amount subject to CIS.

scope: contractor; UK; releasing a retention to a subcontractor who now has gross status
rules: Retention payments follow the normal CIS rules, using the subcontractor's status on the date of payment, not the date of the work.
Re-verification is needed unless the subcontractor was on a return in the current or two previous tax years.

scope: contractor; UK; missed CIS deductions for one subcontractor
rules: The contractor is liable for deductions it failed to make, but HMRC can direct that it need not pay if it took reasonable care and the failure was a good-faith error or it genuinely believed CIS did not apply, or the subcontractor was not taxable on the money or has paid his tax.
If HMRC refuses the direction, the contractor can appeal within 30 days of the refusal.

scope: limited company subcontractor; UK; reclaiming CIS deducted by main contractors
rules: A company sets the CIS deducted from it against its PAYE, NI, student loan and CIS liabilities for the period, reported on the EPS, carrying any surplus forward within the same tax year.
After the tax year ends and final returns are in, any remaining deductions can be repaid or set against Corporation Tax.

scope: contractor with gross payment status; UK; failing the annual gross status review
rules: If HMRC confirms cancellation, gross status ends 90 days after the notice, and the company can appeal within 30 days, with an appeal delaying cancellation until decided.
After a normal cancellation the company must wait one year to reapply; after an immediate cancellation for false information, fraud or knowing failures the wait is five years.

scope: contractor; UK; supply chain CIS or PAYE fraud below it
rules: From 6 April 2026, a contractor that knew or should have known that someone in the supply chain was deliberately failing to deduct or pay CIS or PAYE can be made liable for 20% of the payment it made.
A penalty of up to 30% of that amount can follow, and part or all of a company's penalty can be passed to a responsible director.
Gross payment status can be cancelled with immediate effect, with a five-year bar on reapplying.

scope: contractor; UK; paying a county council highways team for a road crossing
rules: From 6 April 2026 a payment to a local authority or a listed public body is not a contract payment under CIS, so it is not verified, not deducted and not reported on the monthly return.

scope: contractor; UK; carpet fitting on a show flat
rules: Carpet fitting is outside CIS, so no deduction is made; fitting vinyl, lino or laminate floors to finish a building is inside the scheme.

scope: contractor; UK; scaffolding hire and scaffold erection
rules: Hiring scaffolding without labour is outside CIS.
Erecting and dismantling scaffolding is a construction operation inside CIS.

scope: contractor taking workers from a labour agency; UK; not stated
rules: A payment to an agency whose workers do construction work under their contracts with it is a CIS contract payment, unless off-payroll (IR35) rules apply to the engagement.

An employment business supplying workers paid on timesheets at hourly or daily rates under the customer's direction is supplying staff, not construction services, so the VAT reverse charge does not apply and it charges VAT normally.

scope: contractor paying a roofing subcontractor with gross payment status; UK; roofing work
rules: The VAT reverse charge applies where both parties are VAT registered, the payment is reported under CIS and the work is a specified construction service, whatever the supplier's CIS payment status (gross or under deduction).

scope: contractor working for a housing association client; UK; not stated
rules: The end user exception to the reverse charge applies only if the customer confirms in writing that it is an end user, no later than the time of supply or in the written contract; without that notice the supplier keeps applying the reverse charge.

scope: contractor using a subcontractor; UK; CCTV and alarm installation with trenching and concrete posts
rules: Installing security systems alone is outside the reverse charge, but where it forms a single supply with specified services such as groundworks, the whole supply is reverse charged.
Where the specified services are no more than 5% of the contract value, the parties may agree at the outset to disregard them; this is optional and not judged invoice by invoice.

scope: developer building new houses for sale, using a groundworks subcontractor; UK; new dwellings
rules: The reverse charge covers only standard-rated and reduced-rated construction services, not zero-rated ones.
Groundworks done in the course of constructing a new dwelling are zero-rated.

scope: builder working for a homeowner; UK; new detached house built after demolishing a bungalow
rules: A building constructed after an existing building has been demolished completely to ground level counts as a new building for zero-rating.
The new building must meet the dwelling conditions: self-contained, usable and disposable separately, and built in line with planning consent.
Only services that are part of the building works qualify; excluded items such as professional fees and plant hired without an operator are not zero-rated.

scope: builder; UK; renovation of a terraced house empty for three years
rules: Renovating a dwelling that has not been lived in for at least 2 years before work starts can be charged at the 5% reduced rate.
Evidence of the empty period can come from electoral roll or council tax records, utility companies or the council's Empty Property Officer, and a letter from that officer is enough on its own.
Some items stay standard-rated, such as carpets, fitted wardrobes, scaffolding, hire of goods, landscaping and professional fees.

scope: builder supplying the new owner; UK; refurbishment of a previously empty house now occupied
rules: Work on a dwelling that is lived in when work starts is normally standard-rated.

For a single household dwelling, 5% still applies if it was empty for two years before purchase, no renovation was done in that period, the work is supplied directly to the owner and is done within one year of the purchase; a subcontractor on the job must charge the standard rate.

scope: contractor fitting kitchens; UK; new-build flats
rules: On a zero-rated new dwelling only building materials, such as fitted kitchen units, take the zero rate; appliances such as fridges, freezers and dishwashers are not building materials and are standard-rated.
A cooker counts as a building material only if it is designed to heat the space or water.

scope: contractor paying a subcontractor; UK; not stated
rules: Where the contract sets no period, a pay less notice must be given at least 7 days before the final date for payment, or the notified sum must be paid in full.
A pay less notice must state the sum the payer considers due and the basis on which it is calculated.

scope: subcontractor owed money by a main contractor; UK; not stated
rules: If the payer does not give a payment notice, the payee may give its own notice of the sum due and its basis at any time afterwards, and the final date for payment moves back by the number of days the payee's notice was late.
Where the contract allowed the payee to apply before the due date and it did, that application counts as the payee's notice.
The payer must pay the notified sum by the final date unless it gives a valid pay less notice.

scope: main contractor with a pay-when-paid subcontract; UK; not stated
rules: A clause making payment conditional on the payer receiving payment from a third party is ineffective unless that third party, or someone further up the chain, is insolvent; if no other terms are agreed, the Scheme's payment provisions apply.

scope: subcontractor unpaid by a main contractor past the final date; UK; not stated
rules: If the notified sum is not paid by the final date, the payee may suspend some or all of its work after giving at least 7 days' written notice of its intention and the grounds.
The right to suspend ends when payment is made in full; the payer must pay the reasonable costs of suspension, and the suspension period is added to the time for completion.

scope: contractor in a payment dispute; UK; not stated
rules: The adjudicator must be appointed and the dispute referred within 7 days of the notice of adjudication.
The decision is due within 28 days of referral, extendable to 42 days with the referring party's consent or longer if both parties agree.
The decision binds the parties until the dispute is finally settled by legal proceedings, arbitration or agreement.

scope: contractor; England; council repair contract worth about 25,000 pounds
rules: For a council (not central government), a below-threshold contract is notifiable only at 30,000 pounds or more including VAT; below that no tender or contract details notice is required.
Where a notifiable contract is advertised, the tender notice must be published on Find a Tender before anywhere else.

scope: local contractor; England; council small works tender
rules: Councils may reserve below-threshold competitions to suppliers based in the UK or in a local area, which is the council's own area optionally with neighbouring counties or London boroughs, and this must be stated in the tender notice or advert.
Being based in an area means having substantive operations there, regardless of ownership, and competitions may also be reserved to SMEs.

scope: contractor bidding for council work; England; not stated
rules: The thresholds that apply from 1 January 2026 do not affect a procurement that had already begun before that date, and publishing a tender notice counts as beginning it.

scope: contractor with 30 staff and 6 million pounds turnover; England; council tenders reserved for SMEs
rules: An SME has fewer than 250 staff and either a turnover of 44 million pounds or less or a balance sheet total of 38 million pounds or less.

scope: contractor new to public work; UK; council tenders
rules: Suppliers register free on the central digital platform (Find a Tender) using a GOV.UK One Login account, registering the organisation with its Companies House number or a platform identifier.
Suppliers must complete their supplier information (such as connected persons, exclusion grounds and financial details) and share their unique identifier with the buyer before award.

scope: not stated; UK; not stated
rules: The reverse charge applies to standard or reduced-rated construction services supplied between VAT-registered businesses where the payment is reported under CIS.
It does not apply to workers supplied by an employment business, to zero-rated work, to supplies within a VAT group, or where the customer has given written end user or intermediary notice.

scope: contractor paying a subcontractor; UK; not stated
rules: The contract's own due dates and final dates for payment apply if adequate; if it is silent, the Scheme applies and the final date is 17 days after each due date.
In a sub-contract under a public contract covered by the Procurement Act, payment within 30 days of receiving the invoice is implied.

scope: contractor; England; council job of unstated value
rules: Below the procurement thresholds (works 5,193,000 pounds from 2026) a council has wide freedom, including asking chosen suppliers for quotes or making a direct award, subject to its own rules.
If a council advertises a below-threshold contract worth 30,000 pounds or more, it must first publish a tender notice.

scope: main builder; England; domestic job with a second contractor engaged by the homeowner
rules: Where more than one contractor is involved, the client must appoint a principal contractor and a principal designer in writing.

If a domestic client does not appoint them, the contractor in control of the construction work becomes principal contractor and the designer in control of the design phase becomes principal designer, and the principal contractor takes on the client duties.
Where more than one contractor is involved, a health and safety file must be prepared.

scope: builder with four workers; England; six-week loft conversion
rules: A project must be notified to HSE only if it is expected to last over 30 working days with over 20 workers on site at the same time, or to exceed 500 person days.
CDM duties, including the construction phase plan, apply whether or not the project is notifiable.

scope: contractor; England; large notifiable domestic project
rules: For a domestic client, the duty to notify passes to the contractor (single contractor) or the principal contractor, or to the principal designer if agreed in writing.
Notice must be given to HSE as soon as practicable before the construction phase starts.
A current copy of the notice must be displayed in the site office where workers can read it, and updated if it changes.

scope: single contractor; England; one-week domestic bathroom refit
rules: Every project needs a construction phase plan, and where there is only one contractor it must draw up the plan before setting up the site.
The plan must be proportionate to the risks; for small domestic work a short plan is enough.

scope: contractor; England; non-notifiable project
rules: CDM requirements, including the construction phase plan, welfare and induction, apply whether or not the project is notifiable; notification only adds the duty to notify HSE.

scope: contractor taking on new workers; England; construction site
rules: Every worker must receive a site-specific induction from the principal contractor, or from their own contractor where the principal contractor has not given one.

The induction should cover the site's particular risks and controls, an outline of the project and its management, first aid, accident reporting, worker consultation and each person's responsibilities.
Workers must be told the procedure to follow in serious and imminent danger.

scope: Romanian worker of a contractor; UK; work on a scaffold
rules: Employers must have procedures that let workers stop work and go immediately to a place of safety in serious and imminent danger, and workers may raise concerns with the employer or HSE without penalty.
Workers must report dangers they identify to the employer or the person in control.

scope: contractor's worker on an 8-hour site shift; UK; construction site
rules: A worker working more than 6 hours in a row is entitled to a rest break of at least 20 minutes.

scope: contractor; England; domestic job using the homeowner's facilities
rules: Welfare facilities may be provided or made available, so existing facilities can be used if they meet the required standards, are readily accessible, and are checked as suitable and kept in good order.
Welfare facilities must be in place before work starts and maintained until the end of the project.

scope: main contractor with several subcontractors; England; construction site
rules: The principal contractor must ensure the required welfare facilities are provided for the whole construction phase.
Each contractor must, so far as reasonably practicable, provide welfare facilities for its own workers.

scope: contractor; not stated; construction site
rules: Toilets must be suitable and sufficient and readily accessible, with the number depending on the headcount, and chemical or self-contained flushing toilets may be used where mains drainage is not possible.

scope: contractor using ladders; UK; not stated
rules: A ladder should be set at an angle of 1 out for every 4 up.
An access ladder should extend at least 1 m above the landing point to give a handhold.
A ladder should be secured against slipping by tying both stiles, or else by a stability device or wedging; footing is the last resort.

scope: contractor; not stated; not stated
rules: A ladder may be used only for short-duration, low-risk work where more suitable equipment is not justified.

A ladder must have a pre-use check and periodic detailed inspections, stand on firm level footing, and have no damaged stiles, rungs or feet; household DIY ladders are generally not suitable for site work.

scope: contractor using an aluminium mobile tower; UK; indoor work
rules: A mobile working platform does not need a new inspection each time it is moved on the same site, provided it has been inspected on that site within the last 7 days.
If guard rails or other parts are removed and replaced, a trained user should carry out a pre-use check.

scope: contractor using a mobile tower; UK; not stated
rules: A tower must never be moved with people or materials on it.
Before moving, the tower should be reduced to no more than 4 m and the route checked for overhead hazards and firm, level ground without holes.

scope: contractor; UK; gutter work on a domestic garage with a corrugated cement sheet roof
rules: Unreinforced cement sheeting is likely to be fragile, and a roof should be treated as fragile until a competent person confirms otherwise.
No one may pass across or near a fragile surface where the work can be done safely another way; if not, platforms or coverings, fall-limiting measures and warning notices are required.

scope: contractor using harnesses; UK; work at height
rules: Planning work at height must include planning for emergencies and rescue, with a set rescue procedure that workers know, rather than relying on the emergency services.

scope: contractor cutting concrete blocks with a disc cutter; UK; not stated
rules: The employer must assess the risk from hazardous substances such as respirable crystalline silica and prevent or adequately control exposure, using other controls such as water suppression or on-tool extraction first and RPE in addition, not instead.
Exposure to respirable crystalline silica must be kept below 0.1 mg/m3 as an 8-hour time-weighted average.

scope: not stated; UK; not stated
rules: The workplace exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica is 0.1 mg/m3 as an 8-hour time-weighted average.
For carcinogens, exposure must be reduced as low as reasonably practicable, not only kept below the limit.

scope: contractor using a 110V electric cut-off saw; UK; not stated
rules: Water suppression must not be used on electric cut-off saws; these need on-tool extraction, and wet cutting is for petrol or non-electric saws.

scope: employer of workers wearing dust masks; UK; not stated
rules: Tight-fitting respirators must be face-fit tested by a competent person, with retesting if the mask or the wearer's face changes.
A tight-fitting mask does not protect a wearer who is not clean-shaven where it seals; loose-fitting powered hoods or visors do not need fit testing and suit bearded workers.

scope: employer with a workshop dust extraction unit; UK; workshop
rules: Local exhaust ventilation must be thoroughly examined and tested by a competent person at least once every 14 months.
Records of examinations, tests and repairs must be kept for at least 5 years.

scope: contractor; UK; stripping flaking paint from sash windows in a 1930s house
rules: Paint on older buildings should be assumed to contain lead, which was used in house paints until the 1960s.
Lead paint should be removed by chemical stripper, wet abrasion or on-tool extraction, with hot air guns kept below 500 C and no blowlamps or gas torches.
Workers need disposable overalls, an FFP3 mask and proper washing facilities with hot or warm water to wash before eating, drinking or smoking.

scope: employer; UK; not stated
rules: At the lower exposure action values (80 dB(A) daily or 135 dB(C) peak) the employer must make hearing protection available on request.
At the upper exposure action values (85 dB(A) or 137 dB(C)) the employer must provide hearing protection, mark hearing protection zones and ensure it is worn there.
The exposure limit values of 87 dB(A) and 140 dB(C), taking account of hearing protection, must not be exceeded.

scope: employer without a noise meter; UK; not stated
rules: An employer must assess noise risk where workers are likely to be exposed at or above the lower exposure action value.
If people have to shout to be heard at 2 m for more than about 2 hours a day, the noise is likely around 85 dB(A) and an assessment is needed.

scope: employer; UK; construction site with about 15 workers
rules: Every site needs a suitably stocked first-aid box, a person appointed to take charge of first aid and information telling workers the arrangements.
For 5 to 50 workers on a construction site, at least one trained first aider is suggested, with first-aid provision based on a needs assessment.
The employer must arrange necessary contacts with external emergency services.

scope: employer of an injured worker; UK; not stated
rules: A fracture other than to a finger, thumb or toe is a specified injury that must be reported to HSE.
Reportable accidents must also be recorded, for example in an accident book.

scope: employer of an injured worker; UK; not stated
rules: An injury is reportable when the worker is away from work or unable to do normal work for more than seven consecutive days, not counting the day of the accident.
An injury causing more than three consecutive days' incapacity must be recorded, but not reported.

scope: small builder; UK; not stated
rules: Since 2013, an over-seven-day incapacity (excluding the day of the accident) is the trigger for reporting an injury; over-three-day injuries must be recorded but not reported.

scope: contractor; UK; site with an overhead power line
rules: Plant or equipment coming into contact with an overhead power line is a reportable dangerous occurrence even if no one is hurt.
Plant should be kept at least 15 m plus the jib length from lines on steel towers and 9 m plus the jib length from lines on wooden poles, unless the line is made dead, diverted or shrouded.
Overhead lines must be diverted or isolated, or, where that is not reasonably practicable, protected with barriers and warning notices.

scope: contractor; UK; domestic job using house sockets
rules: Cordless tools or a 110V centre-tapped supply are preferred on site.
Where 230V mains tools are used, they must be protected by an RCD rated at 30 mA or less with no time delay, tested daily with its test button.

scope: builder using a plumber for gas work; Great Britain; not stated
rules: Anyone doing gas work must be competent, and a self-employed gas engineer or the employer must be a member of the HSE-approved class of persons, currently the Gas Safe Register.
A person who controls gas work must take reasonable steps to ensure the person doing it is registered.

scope: installer; Great Britain; new gas boiler in a domestic en-suite
rules: A gas appliance may be installed in a room containing a bath or shower only if it is room-sealed.
Gas installation work must be done by a member of the approved class of persons (Gas Safe registered).

scope: builder using a plumber; Great Britain; unspecified gas job
rules: Work on gas fittings must be done by a competent person who is, or works for, a member of the approved class (Gas Safe registered), with limited exceptions such as replacing hoses or regulators on portable appliances and cylinders.

scope: employer with 15 employees; UK; not stated
rules: An employer must prepare, keep up to date and bring to employees' attention a written statement of its health and safety policy and the organisation and arrangements for carrying it out.
An employer with five or more employees must record its health and safety arrangements and the significant findings of its risk assessment.

scope: employer taking on a 17-year-old apprentice; UK; not stated
rules: Before employing a young person, the employer must make or review a risk assessment that takes account of their inexperience, immaturity and lack of risk awareness, the equipment they will use and their training.
Employees must be given health and safety training when recruited.

scope: contractor; England; construction workers
rules: A contractor must not employ or appoint a person on site unless they have, or are gaining, the skills, knowledge, training and experience needed for the work.
Employers must give health and safety training on recruitment and when risks change, such as new equipment or new responsibilities.

scope: builder; England; 4 m single storey rear extension to a semi-detached house
rules: For a house that is not detached, a single storey rear extension is permitted development up to 3 m beyond the original rear wall and up to 4 m high.

Beyond 3 m and up to 6 m it needs the prior approval (neighbour consultation) process, and work cannot start until the council says approval is not needed, grants it, or 42 days pass without a decision.
On article 2(3) land (such as a conservation area) or a SSSI the limit stays 3 m, so 4 m needs a planning application.

scope: contractor for a council; England; replacing timber sash windows with uPVC on houses in a conservation area
rules: Replacing windows on a house can be permitted development under Class A, provided the materials give a similar appearance to the existing house; uPVC can qualify if the windows look similar in shape and frame colour and size.
A local planning authority can remove permitted development rights with an Article 4 direction (common in conservation areas), so check with it first; if removed, a planning application is needed.
